scene.testo: After the war, British interrogators asked Germany's former Commander in Chief in the West a simple question. Why did D-Day succeed? The answer he gave was short. He used the same two words three times.

Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt said it was a matter of air power, air power, and again air power. He said Allied aircraft made it impossible for his tanks to move. The records show he was largely right.

But the official United States Army history of the invasion documents something his answer left out. On the morning of June 6, 1944, thick clouds covered Normandy. Two German panzer divisions could have moved under that cover.

They did not move. The reason was not Allied aircraft. It was an order from Hitler's own headquarters. And what Rundstedt did when it reached him is the part of the story he never told his interrogators.
Rundstedt was the oldest of Hitler's field marshals. He had been a soldier for more than fifty years. Since 1942, he had held the supreme command in the West, from a headquarters near Paris.

His task was clear above all others. Stop the invasion everyone knew was coming. Along the Atlantic coast, thousands of men worked on concrete bunkers, beach obstacles, and guns. This was the wall he was meant to defend.

On May 1, 1945, an American patrol captured him in Bavaria. He was sixty-nine years old. Germany was collapsing around him. The man who had commanded the West was now a prisoner, sitting before his captors.
He is recorded as saying it was a disgraceful position for a soldier to surrender without a fight. That summer he was handed over to the British. There, the questions began.
His first answer was about his tanks. He said that if he had been able to move the armored divisions behind the coast, he was convinced the invasion would not have succeeded. It was a bold claim.
If those armored divisions could have moved, Normandy might have become Dieppe on a vast scale. A disaster on the beach. Instead, Allied aircraft did three things that he said decided the outcome.

They wrecked the railway junctions. They hunted every road and every column until daytime movement became impossible. And they dropped carpets of bombs in front of American and British troops, clearing the way.
scene.q: bombers dropping bombs on rail yards

scene.testo: He added that the few German aircraft in the sky were outnumbered by as much as ten to one. The records support much of what he said. And the campaign began well before the invasion.
On May 7, 1944, Allied bombers began striking the bridges over the Seine. By May 26, every railway crossing over the river north of Paris was closed. They stayed closed for thirty days.

After D-Day, the bridges over the Loire were destroyed as well. On June 13, the supply officer of the German Seventh Army reported that rail traffic had been paralyzed by ninety percent since the invasion.
Normandy had been cut off from the rest of France from the air. So the panzers had to travel by road. And on the roads, the Allied air forces were waiting for them in the open daylight.
scene.q: German column road air attack Normandy

scene.testo: One of the best divisions in the German army, Panzer Lehr, was ordered to the front in broad daylight. Its commander, General Fritz Bayerlein, described that day afterward. By noon, he said, the situation was terrible.
His men, he said, called the main road a fighter-bomber racecourse. By the end of the day he had lost forty fuel trucks and ninety other vehicles. Field Marshal Erwin Rommel recorded the same thing.

Rommel, commanding the coast, wrote that during the day almost all of the army's movement was paralyzed. On July 17, he was himself badly wounded on a Normandy road when low-flying Allied aircraft attacked his car.

So Rundstedt's explanation holds up. Air power did strangle the German response. But now return to the morning of June 6. Because the official record shows a moment that happened before any aircraft could interfere.
Between 3:30 and 4:00 that morning, two hours before the seaborne landings began, Rundstedt acted. He ordered the 12th SS Panzer Division to move toward Caen, and Panzer Lehr to prepare to follow.
The official history describes his reasoning as clear and his action as decisive. But there was a problem. Neither division was under his direct command. They belonged to Hitler's reserve.

At about 7:30, General Jodl at Hitler's headquarters told him the divisions could not move without Hitler's order. According to the official history, Rundstedt accepted this without objection. He made no effort to reach Hitler himself.

The two divisions waited, away from the beaches, through the morning hours. The weather stayed heavily overcast. According to the history, that cloud cover would have let them advance with little interference from Allied aircraft.

At four in the afternoon, Hitler finally gave the green light. By then, the clouds had cleared. Allied fighters and bombers were destroying anything that moved. The advance had to wait until after dark.
The bulk of the two divisions did not reach the battlefield until June 8. By then the Allies had two full days to land men, tanks, and supplies. The beachhead was no longer fragile.
scene.q: Allied troops supplies landing beach Normandy

scene.testo: After the war, Rundstedt told this part differently. He said higher-ranking officers interfered with the placement of his forces. And when he was finally able to move them, he said, it was already too late.
By then, he claimed, Allied aircraft had destroyed his reinforcements completely. As commander in chief in the West, he told one interviewer, his only authority was to change the guard at his gate.

Yet he knew the Atlantic Wall could be broken. In October 1943, he had warned that victory in the West depended on fast, powerful counterattacks. On June 6, the divisions meant for that counterattack waited for Hitler's permission.
So, was Rundstedt right? About Allied air power, yes. The evidence from Normandy shows how severely it restricted every German movement. But air power was not the entire story.
On the morning of June 6, Rundstedt moved quickly. When Hitler's headquarters stopped his orders, he did not object. He made no effort to reach Hitler. The clouds lasted for hours. Then they cleared.
No one can know whether an early counterattack would have changed D-Day. But the official record shows something his postwar explanations did not. He knew his reserves had to move fast.
And when his orders were stopped, he did not take the last step that was still open to him. Air power was real. It was decisive. But on that morning, the loss of time was a German decision.

Rundstedt was not the only German commander questioned after the war. Many of Hitler's generals sat before Allied interrogators, and each gave an account shaped by defeat, memory, and the wish to explain.

When American officers asked Heinz Guderian about General Patton, his reply repeated what Hitler had said. That story is appearing on your screen now. Subscribe for more of what the men on the other side said in their own words.
The record of D-Day is built from many voices. Rundstedt's is one of them. Read beside the documents, it reveals both what he saw clearly, and what he chose to leave unsaid. Watch the next video.

descrizione:
After the war, British interrogators asked Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt why D-Day succeeded. His answer used the same two words three times: air power. This documentary compares his postwar testimony with the official records of Normandy.

We examine the bombing of the Seine bridges, the destruction of German rail traffic, the ordeal of Panzer Lehr, and the morning of June 6, 1944, when two panzer divisions waited for Hitler's permission to move while the clouds still covered Normandy.
